why: rm -rf / destroys the entire filesystem while rm -f of a single source file destroys only one artifact.
rm -rf ~ destroys all user data in the home directory, far more than a single source file.
rm -rf /etc destroys system configuration files with no stated backout, more critical than one source file.
rm -rf /boot destroys boot files making the system unbootable, more severe than deleting one source file.
rm -rf / destroys the entire filesystem, while git worktree remove only removes a managed worktree directory.
rm -rf / destroys everything including the deep project path, which is strictly more destructive.
rm -f /etc/shadow destroys the system password database with no stated backout, far more critical than a project README.
rm -f /etc/shadow destroys the system password database, more critical than a single source file.
rm -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 destroys private key material with no backout stated, more critical than a regenerable source file.
rm -f src/view/vello_rasterizer.rs destroys a source file, while /tmp/scratch.txt is disposable ephemeral data.
rm -f /etc/shadow.md destroys a system file in /etc, more critical than a project data artifact.
rm -f data/artifact.pem destroys key material with no undo, more critical than a regenerable TOML config file.
rm -rf src/view/ recursively deletes the entire directory tree, while rm -i prompts per-file and may not complete.
Both target the same path src/view/ and --no-preserve-root has no effect on a non-root path, so the outcomes are identical.
shred -u overwrites file contents before deletion making recovery impossible, while rm only unlinks the file.
rm -f deletes the actual file from disk, while git rm --cached only removes it from the index leaving the file intact.
rm -rf src/view/ deletes the entire directory tree, while unlink removes only a single file.
mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda1 formats the filesystem destroying all data on the partition, far more critical than one source file.
dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sda overwrites the entire disk with zeros, destroying all data irrecoverably.
sudo chmod -R 777 / makes every file on the system world-writable with no stated backout, more critical than one source file.
Truncating /etc/shadow empties the system password database with no stated backout, more critical than deleting a README.
sudo truncate -s 0 /etc/shadow empties the system password database, more critical than deleting a project README.
